utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber has not heard of any preliminaries to be raised. There is one request. Mr. Stojanovic, I don't think we already received an estimate of the time for cross-examination of the witness, the next witness. Do you have one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. We have conveyed this to the Prosecution and we expect this to last up to two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We heard possibly two and a half hours on our list with a question mark so that's triggered up to two hours. That's up to two and a half hours. No, up to two hours, you said, yes. Then in view of the fact that protective measures apply for the next witness, we have to move into closed session to allow the witness to enter the courtroom but before we do so, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we do that, the witness after this witness is expert Robert Donia. On Monday the Defence filed a written application raising a number of issues. The Prosecution would ask an opportunity to address those issues orally prior to the start of that witness and we anticipate it would take 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would you consider that we should wait until after we have finished the witness next to be called.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it's not entirely clear -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, do we understand that your oral submissions would amount to a response to the decision on relating to expert witness Robert Donia? Or is it related to this matter raised by the Defence on which the Chamber would like to decide before the witness starts his examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then why not do it right away so that we have an opportunity to consider that at least during the break? Of course, you'll understand that we started thinking about the application made by the Defence and the sooner we know what the position of the Prosecution is, the better it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles will be addressing the Chamber on this matter. I can have her --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then -- if she would do that the last 10 to 15 minutes before the end of the first session this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So on from quarter past 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we turn into closed session in order to allow the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Witness RM249, when you entered the courtroom, the curtains were down because you'll testify with protective measures; that is, first, we will not use your own name and we will avoid any reference to who you are. Second, no one outside this courtroom will see your face. Having explained this, before you give evidence the rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which will now be handed out to you by the usher. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness 249. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you'll first be examined by Mr. Vanderpuye, who is counsel for the Prosecution. You'll find him to your right. Mr. Vanderpuye, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you, Your Honours, good morning everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Before we get started I just want to remind you to try to keep your voice up, try to speak a little bit more slowly than you would normally, which will allow the interpreters to convey perhaps more accurately what you say in response to the questions that I ask you, and also let me know if there is anything that I've asked that is unclear and I'll do my best to try and rephrase it so we can better understand one another. Let me first start by showing you 65 ter 30175.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I'll ask you, sir, to have a look at this document and without saying what's on it, if you can confirm that you are the person named in it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: Yes. I am the person mentioned in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President I would tender this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 30175 will be Exhibit P1989 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1989 is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall having provided a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor dated 24 January 1996?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember giving a statement on this particular date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you also recall having testified in the case of Prosecutor versus Tolimir on the 18th of March 2010?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: Yes. I equally remember appearing as a witness in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were your testimony and statement truthful when you gave them respectively?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: Yes, they were completely truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review both your statement from 24 January 1996 and the testimony that you provided in the Tolimir case prior to testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: Yes. I have had such an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in the case of your testimony, did you have an opportunity to listen to the audio recording of your appearance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: Yes, I did that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Having reviewed your testimony and your 24 January 1996 statement can you confirm that they reflect what you said on those occasions respectively?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: Yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do they fairly and accurately reflect what you would say if you were to be examined here today and I were to put to you those same questions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, it would be identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President at this time I would tender both the statement and the testimony under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but before we proceed, I think we need 65 ter numbers. But before doing so, Witness, you said for the most part it would be identical. Did you mean to say that in substance it would be identical or is there any part where you distance yourself from it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't distance myself from it. I said that the entire statement is fully and completely truthful and accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Vanderpuye, the 65 ter numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The 65 ter number for the statement is 30176. I would tender it under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 30176 will be Exhibit P1990 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1990 is admitted under seal. The excerpt of the transcript, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It is 65 ter number 30177.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 30177 will be Exhibit P1991, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also under seal, I take it? There is no need to do that? Let me just check. Yes. It is in open session. Then P1991 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would also tender the associated exhibits at this time that are referenced in the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. Could you give us the 65 ter numbers for them?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. 65 ter 05024.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I first ask, Mr. Stojanovic, is there any objection against any of the associated exhibits? No, there is not. Or is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Vanderpuye, if you read the 65 ter number then the Registrar will immediately assign a number to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. They are 65 ter numbers 05024.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1992, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1992 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1993, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1993 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1994 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1995, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1995 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1996, I assume under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1996 admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the last document I plan to use with the witness, so I won't be tendering it at this time. I hopefully will be able to have enough time to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I have a summary of the witness's statement or evidence I'd like to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You explained to the witness the purpose of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness it will be read so that the public knows more or less what is in your written statement, which allows the public to better understand the remainder of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The witness moved to Srebrenica in 1983. Soon after the war broke out, he was wounded in a shelling incident and suffered a serious shrapnel injury. In July 1995, the witness lived in Srebrenica with his family. They left Srebrenica on 11 July for Potocari seeking the protection of UNPROFOR. When the witness and his family arrived in Potocari, they took refuge in a building where they spent the night. On 12 July, when the removal of the population began, the witness recognised many people he knew. Realising that Serb soldiers were separating men from their families, he searched for a place to hide. He eventually found a group of broken down buses to which he and his family moved during the night. In the early morning of 13 July, the witness's wife went to get water. When she returned she told the witness that she had seen blood on the ground floor of one of the houses nearby. They decided to try to leave Potocari and join the crowd of refugees trying to do the same around 8.00 a.m. that morning. The witness carried his young daughter through to a check-point where he waited for his wife and mother who had fallen behind. They eventually managed to get on to or into an overcrowded bus through the back door. The witness sat on the floor to avoid detection. The bus left Potocari proceeding in the direction of Bratunac and was soon stopped at Magasici. The witness could hear someone outside asking whether there were any men on the bus. The bus then travelled toward Kravica then toward Milici, being stopped at both locations. Throughout the journey the bus was similarly stopped about nine or ten times before reaching Luke around 10.00 a.m. At Luke everyone was made to leave the bus. The witness who was carrying his young daughter was ordered to give her over to his wife and he complied. He was taken a short distance to the school by a Serb soldier who said that he recognised the witness from a previous -- from his previous workplace. He warned the witness to answer all questions or he would be beaten. Outside the school, the witness was placed next to another prisoner and subsequently had his hands bound. By dusk, the prisoners numbered about 22. The witness recalled several of their names. Sometime after 9.00 p.m. the prisoners were brought into the school one by one. Inside a classroom, they were searched, had their property taken, and verbally and physically abused by the Serb soldiers. The witness was bloodied by a blow with a pipe to his head. Shortly after midnight, on the morning of 14 July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you switch off -- one second, please, Mr. Mladic, if you consult with counsel, it's better to switch off your microphone, which has now been done. Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Shortly after midnight on the morning of 14 July, the prisoners were ordered on to a military truck. Several armed Serb soldiers also got in. They drove in the direction of Vlasenica before turning off on to a gravel road and continuing to the execution point. There, the soldiers took up positions, began pulling prisoners off the truck and then executing them. Two men were shot trying to escape. But the witness managed to flee under fire and made it to some nearby bushes where he hid behind a rock to avoid being hit. He went down a steep slope, winding up near a stream where he remained in the dark. The witness subsequently heard strong gunfire coming from the area from which with he had fled, lasting about ten minutes. He concluded the remaining prisoners had been killed. He stayed put until dawn and then set out. After two weeks, on 27 July 1995, the witness arrived in the free territory. Mr. President, that concludes my summary and I have a few additional questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed and take care that you finish approximately by quarter past up to 20 minutes past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, at paragraph -- rather at page 2 of your statement, you speak about the injury that you suffered in 1992. This is the shrapnel injury that I've just mentioned. In relation to that injury, were you subsequently able to perform any military activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: Yes. I was wounded by a shell fired from the Serbian side, that happened on the 14th of May 1992. It was a serious wound to the right knee of my leg, so for a long time I was immobile, I was bed ridden in a house of a schoolmate of mine. Later on I was able to walk with one crutch. You asked me whether I was able to be a member of Defence forces in the town of Srebrenica. I can tell you quite frankly and honestly that I wasn't able to do that and neither was I doing it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did that include 1995, the period in which you left Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The entire time that I spent between the date I was wounded until the date I left Srebrenica, I was not engaged as a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to ask you a few questions about the period before you left Srebrenica, and in particular I'd like to focus you, if I could, in the time period between January and July 1995. Could you tell us what the conditions were like living in Srebrenica during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: It is difficult to describe the situation in Srebrenica relating to a total blockade that the town was under. The people of Srebrenica, who were confined there, tried in a variety of ways to survive in the surrounded town, although at that time Srebrenica enjoyed the status of a protected area, all the provisions and everything that was supposed to be implemented was never implemented in Srebrenica and by that I mean the protection of the people of Srebrenica or the supply of food necessary for Srebrenica. Although there were attempts to provide that, convoys were often stopped, turned back, and only partial deliveries were made after they passed the check-point in Bratunac. So all in all, what reached Srebrenica was only what the people who controlled it wished to be delivered to the people. In other words, there was never sufficient food or medical supplies delivered to the surrounded town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, before you continue, the Chamber noticed that this first question was first of all on a matter on which we have heard evidence again and again and again. To that extent, it's very repetitious. Second, you put a very open question to the witness, which understandably leads him to give a long answer. I would like to remind you that you're limited in your time. You announced 30 minutes. And the Chamber is not seeking repetitious evidence on matters on which we heard much and detailed evidence. Please keep that in mind for the 12 to 17 minutes that are left. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was just about to ask another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you decided to leave Srebrenica, did you feel that you had a choice to remain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: It was impossible for me to remain there because the hatred that was growing among the Serb soldiers was such that everyone who lived in the blockaded Srebrenica, should they have decided to remain in Srebrenica, they would have died definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you reached Potocari, and ultimately decided to get on the bus to leave, did you feel at that point that you had any prospect of remaining either there or in Srebrenica or returning at some future point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: No. At that point, one couldn't possibly think about remaining because that would spell definite death. The only place -- way to save one self was to leave Srebrenica. At the time, I was pondering certain options given that I had this severe wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement, and that's at page 8 in the English and page 9 in the B/C/S, you mentioned that you learned of the location where the execution occurred or where were you brought to be executed from others. You indicated in your statement that it was in the area of Rasica Gaj and the Cikotska river. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: Yes. When I managed to escape the shooting by the Serb soldiers, for seven days I walked alone through forested area until I met a group. This group was made up of people who were familiar with this area, and I also recognised the location where we were taken. One man explained to me the name of that place, and that's the name that you mentioned, Rasica Gaj, so it just happened that I came across this man with whom later on I tried to find a way to a free territory. We met at this specific location and he told me that the place was called Rasica Gaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is just ask you a few questions about some of the people that you mention in your statement. First of all, you mentioned a number of names and I wanted to ask you if you first of all can recall those and if you can recall any last names of the people that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: Yes. All the names that I mentioned, some of their last names I did not mention, though, because I cannot remember them even now. If I mentioned them in my statement, I can still remember them to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned two individuals, one named Fuad and someone named Alija, and that's at page 4 of your statement. You mentioned them together. What I wanted to ask you was do you recall those two individuals, and were they related, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: Yes. I remember mentioning these two names that you cited. I clearly remember that when they were brought in during the day when I was brought before them, these two were brothers. A Serb soldier disclosed their names when the two addressed him and greeted them as a neighbour. In return he cursed their mother, stating that they were no longer neighbours, and during a short altercation between them, they told him their names, that they came from a village close to his village, and that their names were Fuad and Alija. Later on, this would be confirmed upon their arrival in the free territory, and by that I mean that they had been brought in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you remember an individual by the name of Rizo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: Yes. I remember Rizo. His last name is Mustafic, and I mentioned that as well. This gentleman worked in the DutchBat in Potocari as an electrician. During the fall of Srebrenica, he happened to be in the capture area where I was. He was brought in and took to be executed in the same manner and he was shot dead there because he never appeared as a live person later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you remember an individual named Azem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: Yes. He was another gentleman who disclosed his identity when questioned by Serb soldiers. The Serb soldiers asked him where he had been wounded. He had a severe wound and moved with difficulty. And he explained about a place in a forest near Srebrenica. They looked suspiciously at him and said that it was possible that he had been wounded in another place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was his last name Becic, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: Yes, yes. His last name was Becic. That's what I said in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just for the Chamber's reference, I would refer the Chamber to Exhibit P1987 and P1727. For the first one, I would refer the Chamber to page 34 in e-court, relative to information provided by Mr. Janc, and in the corresponding site code for the Chamber's reference, to P1727. Witness, I'm almost out of time and what I'd like to ask you is if you would describe for the Chamber what it was like for you when you reached Luke and were told to hand your daughter over to your wife and to go with the soldier.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: It's difficult to describe that situation. Upon -- so the bus arrived to the final destination where everybody had to leave the bus, and the whole time prior to that I was hidden in the bus. I wanted to hide. That was the first reason. And the second reason was that I couldn't stand because my knee was severely injured. So I sat on the floor of the bus the entire time, and when everybody left the bus I had to leave the bus as well. Upon leaving the bus, I saw a lot of Serbian soldiers checking everybody leaving the bus. My daughter was four years old and she was skinny, quite a skinny child, half the weight of other four year olds, and she was quite attached to me, so I was carrying her, and I took her into my arms. Then a Serb soldier said that I had to turn over the child and go with them. I resigned myself to that. I had to do that. And I went with the soldiers. I made a movement with my head to see my daughter for the last time. He pushed me with the rifle and said, "Move forward." And I moved. He addressed a man who sat on an elevation by the road, and he said to him, "Major, where should we go?" And this major, whom he addressed, indicated with his hand that we should go back, and I continued going there with the man who escorted me. At the same time, he said that he knew me, he said, "I know you from somewhere." And then he said, "Do you know me?" I looked at his face and I told him I didn't know him. He said, "You must know me. You just don't remember me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we briefly move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we continued moving into the background from the direction where the buses had come from. We continued walking and moved for some 200 or 250 metres, at which point in time I saw a facility, it was an elementary school. The Serb soldier indicated with his hand that we should go to the yard of the school. On the way there, he said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you there? I think you have, by far, answered the question that was put to you by Mr. Vanderpuye which was focused on the moment where you had to hand over your daughter. Mr. Vanderpuye, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions, I see that my time has expired.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness I want to thank you for appearing and for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249
utterances.text: Thank you for the questions you put to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What about your last exhibit or your last document you wanted to tender and use with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't think I have the time to do it. But I may have the time yet following the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's not the usual way of dealing with those matters, Mr. Vanderpuye. The best way, I don't know how important the document is you want to tender with the witness, but the best way of course is to keep a tight control of the examination-in-chief and to avoid repetition. But Witness, we will take a break now. That break will be approximately half an hour for you. After the break you'll be cross-examined by Defence counsel. But before you leave the courtroom for the break, we first turn into closed session so that no one will see your face when leaving the courtroom. We turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to make one small correction on the record. P1993, what should be uploaded as that exhibit is 65 ter 5248C, which is an excerpt from the photo book of Mr. Ruez. Pages 24 and 25 thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that -- I have -- is that -- does that mean that it's the wrong number? Because on your list I find -- at least on one of your lists I find, yes, 05248C, you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is hereby on the record. Ms. Bibles, Mr. Groome announced that you would address the Chamber in relation to the most recent filing that is the Defence Rule 94 bis notice and objection relative to proposed Prosecution Witness Robert Donia and a motion to amend the 65 ter list. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. Your Honours, in its 94 bis filing for Dr. Donia, the Defence raises four arguments. The first three of these arguments alleging that the Prosecution has failed to identify the field of expertise - Dr. Donia's methodology and bias - don't require much of a response. Dr. Donia has testified here 14 times at ICTY. These transcripts, his reports, his CVs, are well known and have been disclosed. Dr. Donia's most recent CV was disclosed to the Defence on 23 July. I will seek to add his curriculum vitae to the 65 ter list. It has been uploaded as 65 ter 30165. The bottom line with respect to the first three arguments is that these are matters appropriately for cross-examination. However, the Defence argues that there have been breaches of disclosure, which is notably incorrect. All materials cited by Dr. Donia in his footnotes, which are in the OTP system, have been disclosed to the Defence. It is worth noting that Dr. Donia's two reports and appendices were disclosed in English on the 22nd of February, the B/C/S translations were provided on the 12th of April of 2013. In reviewing his Sarajevo report, it is evident that Dr. Donia's research and sources include books, newspapers, open source materials, that are generally used by scholarly historians in their research and particularly for citing events that were known at the time. I should note that the very poor timing of the filing of the Prosecution's 94 bis notice is my responsibility. It was a mistake particularly given that the reports themselves were actually disclosed months prior. I apologise for that. We did modify this week's schedule to allow additional consideration time given that poor timing. The issue central to this discussion today is related only to a small percentage of footnotes in Dr. Donia's Sarajevo report. As this Trial Chamber is aware, ICTY jurisprudence regarding an expert's sources requires that those sources underlying an expert report are clearly indicated and easily accessible, and if not, whether there is prejudice to the accused. In other litigation on these points have largely arisen in the context of expert reports on which an expert has relied on materials that are not available to the public or to the other party such as a VJ insider or someone who has special access to materials are not available to others. Here, that's not the case. These are documents in the public purview. On 25 July, the Defence requested additional documentation regarding the footnotes in this report noting that Dr. Donia does not provide 65 ter numbers in his footnotes. As an outside expert, he does not have the 65 ter numbers and they would not be included in his report. I immediately advised the Defence that we would provide a chart of the footnoted materials with the 65 ter numbers and ERN location numbers, but I advised that there were open source materials that were not in the OTP database. These include less than 60 pages of material which it is important to consider are largely footnoted in background material. 17 pages of these materials are from one page articles in either "Oslobodjenje" or "Slobodna Bosnia." They are referenced by date and title of the article in these newspapers. Twenty seven of these pages are from nine different books which are all referenced by author, title, publisher, and the year of publication. At least five of which are in the ICTY library upon a quick check yesterday. The others include five official documents and a transcript of a Pale TV show. Of those five official documents, one is the 1991 census, which in a different format is on our exhibit list three times and is accessible to the Defence. The other four include a Bosnia gazette, the 1978 statute of Sarajevo, and archived materials from the city of Sarajevo. These are not in the OTP system and are not subject to disclosure. Having reviewed the Defence filing, however, I did ask Dr. Donia whether he had any of these open source materials available to him. He provided them in a PDF format which we have or can give to the Defence this morning. Aside from being publicly available, these materials generally relate to the background portions of Dr. Donia's report. For example, on page 18, in both the English and B/C/S versions of the Sarajevo report, footnote 45 includes three of these sources. It supports this statement in the report which is describing the history of the development of municipalities in Sarajevo. "The city council undertook the most far reaching these expansions in 1977 driven by the need to strengthen and standardise the existing communications networks and infrastructure in advance of the 1984 winter Olympic Games." If this or any other aspect of the report, supported by the open source footnotes, are at issue in this case, then the appropriate remedy is to cross-examine Dr. Donia with respect to his report on those sources. We do not oppose additional cross-examination time for this witness, for the Defence to challenge areas of the report supported by these sources. As to the memorandum cited at the end of the Defence response, we would happily provide the memorandum and the revision to the -- for the Trial Chamber's consideration. The memorandum, which is 16 pages of double spaced material, was initially provided along with Dr. Donia's 94 bis notice over 30 days ago. Last Friday, in preparation for his testimony, Dr. Donia provided an errata sheet containing or correcting the translation of one cited quote in that memorandum along with some small clerical errors. For clarity, he also provided a clean version of the original memorandum with the corrections provided in the text. There are no substantive additions to the additional memorandum. The clean memorandum was simply provided to assist the Defence in their preparation. We have checked with Dr. Donia, realising that there may be a scheduling issue here, regarding any flexibility in his calendar. We have learned that he could be available through next Monday and perhaps next Tuesday, if necessary, for any additional cross-examination based on these materials. We would also offer that if the Defence was to apply later on for Dr. Donia to be recalled, that we would not oppose that application. We would propose that Dr. Donia is here and prepared to testify and that we proceed with his testimony and cross-examination. Where the appropriate remedy for the objections noted in the Defence response is in a full cross-examination, we would make him available obviously for additional cross-examination if that was necessary following his initial testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The instructions that we have in this report, if you start from footnote number 1, you can see that you have a London and New York cited as the sources, footnote number 2, London, Cambridge university, Harvard, New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can order it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO

utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] But we cannot be requested to go around and collect the materials relating to the expert witness report reviewed by the expert witness and that he is referring to. If he is referring to a certain document, we must be given this document. Today we heard from the Prosecution that all the material from the footnote that are in the OTP system have been made available. You heard the Prosecution saying that. But we need all the materials. If an expert witness is going to make reference to something, we must be given that reference. Secondly, I can tell you that if we go to Sarajevo now and try to find some newspaper from the archive, we would not be able be to acquire that. This Defence team has been asking Sarajevo to provide the most trivial information such as statistical data, and we have to wait between six months and one year just for a reply whether they were going to agree to provide us that. Every day we are in negotiations with Sarajevo. It is also said that the focal point of this discussion according to my colleague, Ms. Bibles, is only a small number of documents that have not been disclosed. That is not correct. It's not just a small portion. If you look at the number of pages, that's a vast part of what is being cited here. Easily accessible to the Defence? It's not true. It is almost not accessible at all. Or it might take six months to order the books, as suggested by His Honour Judge Moloto, and then wait for them to arrive and be delivered. If they say that if this is not accessible, it is questionable whether it is to the prejudice of the accused. We also heard a very long explanation of why 65 ter is missing 60 pages of material, crucial material is missing, 80 pages, 27 books, five of which can be found in the library. They admitted that some archive materials are not in the OTP system, so they clearly admitted we haven't disclosed this to you. We heard today that they are prepared, for some of the materials used by Mr. Donia, to supply us with. They did so but we don't know what it contains. Do the Prosecution agree that we apply the same practice in disclosing our materials to them and we are going to request them to give us this answer? Are they expecting us to disclose the materials relating to our expert witnesses in the same fashion? Have the Rules been set in that way, it would have been done so, but this is not what the Rules say. The Rules say that the materials must be disclosed 30 days before an expert witness begins his testimony. Have they fulfilled this obligation? No, they haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, to assist the Chamber, could you provide us with the authorities saying that every single footnote reference that the underlying material to that reference should be disclosed under all circumstances? Because that apparently is the position you're taking, and when you say what is the Prosecution expecting, as far as our experts will be, if it ever comes to that stage, then I take it, and I'm looking to you, Ms. Bibles and to you Mr. Groome, that you would apply the same standards that accessible material, material in the public domain, et cetera, that there is no need to disclose that, if it's footnote material in expert report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We're simply saying that we understand the jurisprudence at the ICTY and we follow that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, that seems to be a vital issue in your debate, on whether every single underlying document should be disclosed and then of course the question in full or not in full. That seems to be the key issue. Could you also expand on that? I was interrupting you but could you not forget that part of the debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm trying to say is that so far I haven't taken part in the trial because I haven't received all the material made in footnotes. I'm talking about the cases that I participated before in this Tribunal. On the other hand, we provided everything that our expert witness made reference to. We have, for example, the Milosevic case, when the issue of accepting Dr. Donia's paragraph - this is on 15 February 2007, paragraph 7 - where it was stated that there was a reference missing of the available source, and that the Chamber would treat this issue as a personal opinion of the witness rather than his expert opinion. So if the OTP is bringing Mr. Donia as a fact witness here, we will see which facts he's familiar with. However, if he's brought here as an expert witness, we demand that the material that he used in preparing his expert report we ask that to be disclosed to us. Otherwise, we demand that the footnotes be removed because frankly speaking at this point in time we are not able to check whether everything that is stated in the footnotes is really accurate and true. That's as far as the disclosure is concerned. The OTP did not want even to tackle the issue whether Mr. Donia is really an expert or not, and whether he had worked as an expert. It was only said that he testified 14 times. Our position is that despite so many appearances, he did not work as an expert in this particular case. As for his methodology, this is not a scientific methodology. He himself said that his terms of reference was to support the indictment, and it is even contained in one of the titles of his reports. In his report, he provided expert opinion about military, psychiatric, psychological, ethnographic, and all manner of issues, demographic, constitutional, legal matters. We believe that he was -- that he was not proposed to testify about that, nor does he have any requisite qualifications to testify about these issues. What is his report about? His report is about the assemblies of Republika Srpska. He dealt with this issue by taking out of the context and according to his own admission he took out of context certain statements and included them into his report in order to corroborate the indictment. We believe that this is not how an independent expert should operate that this Court should take into consideration when deliberating their judgement. He is not here to help the procedure but, rather, to provide support to the indictment. We know that for a long time he worked for the Prosecution in the Kosovo trials, Mr. Milutinovic et al, and that Mr. Coo had been removed and dismissed as an expert witness precisely for that reason. The memorandum that was mentioned at the beginning of Mrs. Bibles' submission is something that we received on Friday, with all the corrections, and the Chamber says that they are not aware of that. Now we hear that they are prepared to provide this as evidence. Has this been properly disclosed to us, if it was given to us on Friday? No, it hasn't. There are other numerous objections that we perhaps don't have enough time today to discuss in relation to Mr. Donia, but we believe if we really want to discuss the issue whether he's an expert or not, the materials must be disclosed in time. And even if that had been done, we believe that on the basis of these two reports and an annex, Mr. Donia cannot qualify as an expert and we believe that this Chamber must not accept him as an expert witness. Thank you.

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell the Court, please, whether you are aware of the humanitarian operation with the code name "Padobran" or parachute?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249

utterances.speaker: WITNESS RM249

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
